🇲🇽🏭 <u>MEXICO TO WASHINGTON: TRADE, NOT SUBMISSION</u>

With Washington complaining about its trade deficit, Sheinbaum says Mexico is studying whether to buy more from the US "instead of buying from other countries" — a negotiation, not a concession. Meanwhile Mexican exports to the US keep breaking records, powered by electronics feeding the American AI and data-center boom.

🇲🇽✊ <u>MEXICO WRITES ITS INDIGENOUS RIGHTS LAW FROM THE GROUND UP</u>

Mexico is building its new General Law on the Rights of Indigenous and Afro-Mexican Peoples by consulting the people it's for: 50 regional assemblies held so far of 82 planned, running Aug 7–Sept 13, with 2,000+ Tsotsil and Tseltal gathering in San Cristóbal alone to weigh land, communal property, and the right to prior consultation. The proposals go to Congress on Oct 12 — the Day of Indigenous Resistance.

🇲🇽🌐🔥 Mexico ships 80% of its exports to one country that reopens the deal every year — the case for diversification writes itself

New numbers lay the trap bare. Roughly 80% of Mexican exports go to the US, and nearly 89% of the $1.5 billion in goods crossing the border each day move under the USMCA. After Trump refused to renew the treaty in July and switched to annual "reviews," new investment froze: greenfield investment collapsed nearly 50% to $24B in 2025, and fresh foreign investment fell another 13% in the first half of 2026.

The fourth round of USMCA talks just wrapped in Washington with the core fight unresolved — the US wants 50% US-specific content in vehicles built in Mexico, a precedent Mexico rejects because it would only tighten. "If we are going to have constant renegotiation until July of next year, let's just turn off the lights," said the head of Mexico's American Chamber of Commerce.

The lesson isn't panic — it's arithmetic. A nation that depends on a single partner willing to rewrite the terms every 12 months isn't secure; it's exposed. Multiplying markets — Asia, the EU, Latin America — isn't disloyalty. It's insurance.

🇲🇽🐉🌐 Mexico sends its top diplomat to Beijing as Washington demands it wall off China

Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco lands in China on September 7 for his first official visit since taking the post in April — meeting counterpart Wang Yi and inaugurating a new Mexican consulate in Chongqing. The timing is the message: the US is pressuring Mexico to roll back its Chinese trade ties and mirror American barriers on Chinese steel and aluminum, right as the USMCA review drags past its deadline.

Beijing isn't hiding the stakes. China says Mexico's 2026 tariffs already hit more than $30 billion of its exports, and it has opened a trade-barrier investigation. Velasco is going anyway — to "strengthen political dialogue and the cooperation agenda," not to sever it.

This is what sovereignty looks like in a multipolar world: a country leaned on by its largest customer, refusing to let that customer pick its other friends. Mexico gains nothing by turning a $30B+ partner into an enemy on Washington's orders. Keeping the door open isn't betrayal — it's leverage.

🇲🇽⚖️ Hecklers tried to shout her down over the Manzanillo port. She put it to a vote — and won the room. "I read a banner saying you don't agree with the port expansion. What we always do is talk. So let's vote — because democracy is what the majority decides. At the end I'll receive them and hear them out." — Claudia Sheinbaum, "Honestidad y resultados", Colima, Sept 5 2026 Facing protests over the Cuyutlán lagoon, Sheinbaum called a show of hands on whether to let the event continue. The majority backed her — and she offered to meet the group afterward.
📸 Honestidad y resultados — Colima — 5 de septiembre de 2026

🚨🇲🇽 Washington wants Mexico to stop the drugs going north. Mexico wants Washington to stop the guns — and the demand — coming south. As the US tries to fold security into the trade negotiation, Mexico is holding the line: the flood of American weapons into Mexico and US drug consumption are Washington's responsibility. "Parallel tracks," Mexican officials insist — cooperation, not subordination.

🇲🇽🌎 Mexico is negotiating Trump's tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos down — on its own terms. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard has flown to Washington twice to meet Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Mexico is even studying buying more US goods to offset its trade surplus — but security stays a separate track. Mexico City won't let it "contaminate" the trade talks. President Sheinbaum says the economy "remains stable and moving forward" despite the tariffs and the oil-price spike from the US-Iran war. "La amistad no significa renunciar a nuestros principios." "Friendship does not mean giving up our principles." — Claudia Sheinbaum

🇲🇽🌊 On the Manzanillo port expansion, facing protesters: "We won't do anything that harms the environment or the fishermen." "Todo lo vamos a hacer bien, consultando a la gente, consultando a los pescadores. No vamos a hacer nada que afecte ni al medio ambiente ni a los pescadores que viven de la pesca en esa zona." "We'll do it all properly, consulting the people, consulting the fishermen. We won't do anything that harms the environment or the fishermen who live from fishing in that zone." — Claudia Sheinbaum, Colima, Sept 5 2026 The expansion of Mexico's busiest Pacific port has drawn protests over the Cuyutlán lagoon. Sheinbaum met the objectors head-on — offering to receive them after the event and pledging consultation with residents and fishers.

🇲🇽✊ "Health is a human right." Colima gets 198 new primary-care clinics — all free. "Todo gratuito, obviamente, porque la salud es un derecho humano." "All free, obviously, because health is a human right." — Claudia Sheinbaum, "Honestidad y resultados", Colima, Sept 5 2026 The 198 community clinics open by January 2027 — each with a doctor, equipment and 60 basic medicines — plus a new IMSS-Bienestar general hospital in Manzanillo. Across Colima, 245,365 people now receive a Bienestar program: 92,288 pensions for the elderly, 22,000 women on Pensión Mujeres Bienestar, and 20,700 new homes announced.
